module_title: Writs, The Golden Triangle, and Classification of DPSPs
introduction: This intermediate tier transitions to the legal mechanics of constitutional enforcement. It breaks down the prerogative Writs, the expanded interpretation of Article 21, and the ideological classification of the Directive Principles.

core_concepts.title: Article 32 & The Five Writs
core_concepts.description:
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'Heart and Soul' of the Constitution because a right is useless without a remedy.
1. Habeas Corpus ('To have the body of'): Protects against illegal detention.
2. Mandamus ('We command'): Issued to a public official/body to perform their legal duty.
3. Prohibition ('To forbid'): Issued by a higher court to a lower court to stop it from exceeding its jurisdiction (issued during pending proceedings).
4. Certiorari ('To be certified'): Issued by a higher court to quash the order of a lower court (issued after an order is passed).
5. Quo Warranto ('By what authority'): Challenges the legality of a person's claim to a public office.

core_concepts.title: The Golden Triangle (Arts 14, 19, 21)
core_concepts.description: These three articles form the bedrock of constitutional liberty. In the *Maneka Gandhi vs. Union of India (1978)* case, the Supreme Court ruled that these articles are not mutually exclusive but interconnected. A law depriving a person of personal liberty (Art 21) must also pass the test of equality (Art 14) and freedom (Art 19).

core_concepts.title: Article 21: Expanding Horizons
core_concepts.description:
Article 21 states: 'No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.'
- The Supreme Court has vastly expanded this to include the Right to a Speedy Trial, Right to Clean Environment, Right to Privacy (K.S. Puttaswamy Case 2017), and Right to Free Legal Aid. It is not just mere animal existence, but the right to live with human dignity.

core_concepts.title: Classification of DPSPs
core_concepts.description:
Though the Constitution does not classify them, jurists categorize DPSPs into three ideological groups:
1. Socialistic: To reduce inequalities and provide welfare (e.g., Art 39 - Equal pay for equal work, Art 41 - Right to work).
2. Gandhian: Based on Gandhi's reconstruction program (e.g., Art 40 - Village Panchayats, Art 43 - Cottage industries, Art 47 - Ban on intoxicating drinks).
3. Liberal-Intellectual: Promoting modern, progressive ideas (e.g., Art 44 - Uniform Civil Code, Art 45 - Early childhood care, Art 50 - Separation of judiciary from executive).

important_entities.name: Reasonable Restrictions (Article 19)
important_entities.significance: Article 19 grants 6 freedoms (Speech, Assembly, Association, Movement, Residence, Profession). However, the State can impose 'reasonable restrictions' on grounds like sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign states, public order, decency, morality, or contempt of court.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A heavily tested caveat: The writ of **Mandamus** CANNOT be issued against the President of India or State Governors, nor can it be issued against a private individual or body.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: H M P C Q (His Majesty's Private Court Questions)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto.

exam_strategy_tips: If a Judiciary/UPSC question asks 'Which case established the Right to Privacy as a Fundamental Right under Article 21?', the definitive answer is **Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) vs. Union of India (2017)**.
